sources.music-cadence-v1: In a major key the dominant chord (V) contains the leading tone, the seventh degree of the scale, which sits a semitone below the tonic. When V moves to the tonic chord (I), the leading tone rises by a semitone to the tonic, which listeners hear as arrival. Adding the minor seventh to make V7 creates a tritone between the chord's third and seventh; resolving it inward to the tonic chord releases that tension. A perfect fifth spans seven semitones. A minor third spans three semitones and a major third four.
sources.music-harmony-v1: In C major the tonic triad is C-E-G, the subdominant (IV) is F major and the dominant (V) is G major, built from G, B and D. Roman numerals name each chord by the scale degree of its root: I for the tonic, IV for the subdominant, V for the dominant and vi for the relative minor.
sources.pg-plans-v1: An index helps when a query reads a small fraction of a table. When a query returns most of the rows, reading the table in order with a sequential scan is cheaper than jumping between the index and the table for each row, because random page reads cost more than sequential ones. The planner estimates how many rows a condition matches from the table's statistics; stale statistics after a large change can make it choose the wrong plan. EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and reports actual row counts and times. A query passes through four stages: the parser checks the SQL text, the rewriter applies rules such as views, the planner chooses a plan, and the executor runs it.
sources.sd-caching-v1: A cache in front of a database serves reads from a copy. When a write changes the database but not the cached copy, readers see stale data until the entry expires or is invalidated. A time-to-live bounds how long a stale entry can live; invalidating or updating the entry on every write narrows the window further. Little's law says the average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends in it. During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.

items.subject: music-theory
items.prompt: Explain why the chord progression V-I sounds final in a major key.

levels.incomplete: Does not mention a note of V resolving to the tonic.
levels.adequate: Says a note of V moves to the tonic without naming it or saying how far it moves.
levels.strong: Names the leading tone (the seventh degree) and says it rises a semitone to the tonic.

levels.incomplete: Says only that it sounds finished.
levels.adequate: Says V is unstable or tense and I is stable.
levels.strong: Says why V is tense (the leading tone, or the tritone in V7) and that moving to I resolves it.

key_points: the leading tone rises a semitone to the tonic
V, or V7 with its tritone, is unstable and resolves on I
items.reference_answer: The dominant chord contains the leading tone, a semitone below the tonic. When V moves to I the leading tone rises a semitone to the tonic, which we hear as arrival, and the tension of V, especially the tritone in V7, resolves into the stable tonic chord.
items.explanation: V holds the leading tone, which pulls a semitone up to the tonic; I is the stable home chord.
items.source_quote: When V moves to the tonic chord (I), the leading tone rises by a semitone to the tonic, which listeners hear as arrival.

items.subject: postgres-performance
items.prompt: Explain why using an index can make a query slower when the query returns most of a table's rows.

levels.incomplete: Gives no reason beyond saying indexes can be slow.
levels.adequate: Says the index adds extra reads or lookups for each row.
levels.strong: Explains that following the index means random page reads for each row, which cost more than reading the table in order.

levels.incomplete: Does not say how Postgres decides.
levels.adequate: Says Postgres may choose a sequential scan instead.
levels.strong: Explains that the planner estimates the matched fraction from statistics and picks the cheaper sequential scan, and that stale statistics can mislead it.

key_points: random page reads per row cost more than one sequential read
the planner estimates selectivity from statistics
items.reference_answer: When a query returns most rows, following the index means a random page read in the table for almost every row, which costs more than reading the whole table in order. The planner estimates the matched fraction from the table's statistics and chooses a sequential scan when it is cheaper; stale statistics can make it pick the index anyway.
items.explanation: Random page reads per row cost more than one sequential pass, and the planner weighs that from its statistics.
items.source_quote: because random page reads cost more than sequential ones

items.subject: system-design
items.prompt: Explain why putting a cache in front of a database can make readers see stale data, and give one way to limit it.

levels.incomplete: Says caches can be wrong without saying when.
levels.adequate: Says the cached copy can differ from the database.
levels.strong: Explains that a write updates the database but not the cached copy, so reads return the old value until the entry expires or is invalidated.

levels.incomplete: Gives no mitigation, or one that does not address staleness.
levels.adequate: Names a mitigation (a time-to-live, invalidation, write-through) without saying what it limits.
levels.strong: Names a mitigation and says how it limits staleness, such as a time-to-live bounding how long a stale entry lives.

key_points: writes change the database but not the cached copy
a TTL or invalidation on write bounds staleness
items.reference_answer: Reads are served from a cached copy, so when a write changes the database without updating the cache, readers get the old value until the entry expires or is invalidated. A time-to-live bounds how long a stale entry can survive, and invalidating or updating the entry on every write narrows the window further.
items.explanation: The copy lags the database after a write; a TTL bounds the lag and invalidation on write narrows it.
items.source_quote: When a write changes the database but not the cached copy, readers see stale data until the entry expires or is invalidated.

items.subject: system-design
items.prompt: A service receives 1,200 requests per second and each request spends 50 ms in it. By Little's law, how many requests are in the service on average?
items.explanation: Arrival rate times time in system: 1,200 per second times 0.05 s is 60.
items.source_quote: Little's law says the average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends in it.
